---
title: "Design decisions"
---


Each of these could reasonably have gone the other way. They are written down
because the reasoning is the part that gets lost, and because anyone changing
the code deserves to know which choices are load-bearing.

## Failing on an unknown version

**Decided:** refuse a newer exchange version; read older ones.

The alternative is to read what you can and ignore the rest. That works right
up to the release where a column changes meaning rather than name, and then it
produces numbers that look fine. Since these numbers end up in publications,
the failure mode has to be loud.

## Uncoded segments are opt-in, not automatic

**Decided:** `qda_units()` only includes segments no coder coded when the
caller passes the `uncoded` export.

Including them silently would be defensible; it is usually the
methodologically right choice, but it would also mean the same call produces
different coefficients depending on which files happen to be at hand.
Requiring the second file makes the decision visible in the code, which is
where a reviewer can see it.

## Multiple coding is set aside and counted

**Decided:** a coder's several codes on one segment make that cell `NA`; the
count is reported as `multi_set_aside`.

Three alternatives were considered: pick the first code (arbitrary), treat the
set as one compound category (invents categories nobody defined), or refuse to
compute anything (unhelpful). Setting aside and counting is the only option
that neither invents data nor hides how much was dropped. The per-code binary
view exists for projects where multiple coding is the norm.

## Monte Carlo instead of exact for large tables

**Decided:** exact Fisher only for two-by-two; `simulate.p.value = TRUE`
beyond that, with a seed, and without disturbing the global generator.

`fisher.test()` on an r-by-c table is only feasible for small counts. Six
codes over five documents with a few hundred codings is already enough to
abort with a workspace error, and this package used to do exactly that: the
old threshold was `prod(dim(tab)) > 100`, which is the wrong criterion,
because the cost depends on the counts rather than the dimensions. Anything
past two-by-two now goes to simulation.

The seed is restored afterwards. A function that quietly reseeds the global
generator breaks every simulation that happens to run after it, and there is a
test for that.

## Inertia share relative to the whole table

**Decided:** `qda_ca()$inertia_share` divides by total inertia, not by the
retained dimensions.

Normalising to the retained dimensions is common and always sums to 100 %,
which reads as *this map shows everything*. This package had that bug, and the
comparison against the Python twin found it. The check that pins it down is
that total inertia must equal the chi-squared statistic over *n*.

## The statistic is reported even when Fisher is used

**Decided:** `qda_chisq()` returns `statistic` and `expected` regardless of
which test was run.

Cramér's V is computed from the chi-squared statistic. If the returned object
only carried the Fisher result, the effect size would be unrecomputable by the
reader, which makes it un-checkable. There is a test asserting that V equals
`sqrt(statistic / (n * (min(dim) - 1)))`.

## The additional permission lives in LICENSE

**Decided:** no separate `LICENSE-EXCEPTION.md`, unlike the other projects.

`License: AGPL-3 + file LICENSE` in `DESCRIPTION` means *the AGPL plus what is
in that file*, so that is where the section 7 permission belongs. A second
document would duplicate it, and duplicated licence text drifts.
`PROVENANCE.md`, `doc/`, `doc-root/`, `site/`, `script/` and
`versions.json` are in `.Rbuildignore`, because `R CMD check` reports
unknown top-level files. They belong to the repository, not the tarball.

## One function per equation

`qda_unitizing_alpha` used to be one long function. It is now four, and the split
follows the paper rather than a line count: `pair_disorder` is equation (16)
for one pair of coders, `observed_disorder` is (17) summing over pairs,
`expected_disorder` is (18), and `qda_unitizing_alpha` combines them into (19).

**The same split exists in [qdaPy](https://qdapy.zotqda.org) and in [qdaZ](https://qdaz.zotqda.org)'s `stats.js`**, with the same
boundaries and matching names. That is the point: the three can still be read
side by side against Krippendorff, which is the only practical way to check
that three languages implement one formula. Splitting one of them alone would
have bought a metric and cost the thing the metric was meant to protect.

Before and after, the two implementations were run over the same eighty random
configurations in all three languages and compared: identical to the last bit.
